status: interim pilot and post-hoc secondary findings; development and prospective work remain
summary: The pilot shows predictable payoff responses, but a simple payoff-dominant equilibrium rule explains much of the apparent learned Brier improvement. Learned probabilities can improve log loss, while family-held-out cooperation and payoff extrapolation fail. The fixed larger and prospective tests are still in progress; broad strategic generalization is not established.
findings: Across held-out structural families, the combined logistic predictor with identities has action-choice Brier 0.172 versus 0.253 for the ordered model-pair average; improvement 0.081, descriptive 95% interval [0.050, 0.114].

The post-pilot secondary equilibrium selector achieves family-held-out Brier 0.146 for action choice, 0.079 for mutual cooperation, and 0.146 for coordination, versus combined-logistic 0.172, 0.310, and 0.161. Its lower action/cooperation Brier shows that gains over the original stationary independent Nash selector do not establish a need for learning. This is a separately labeled retrospective sensitivity analysis.

Combined logistic improves family-held-out log loss for action choice (0.525 versus secondary equilibrium 0.815) and coordination (0.485 versus 0.569), but its ten-bin calibration error is worse for both (0.151 versus 0.079; 0.128 versus 0.066). The log-loss gain reflects fewer costly overconfident mistakes and does not establish uniformly better calibration. Family-held-out cooperation remains worse by both scoring rules. The descriptive paired log-loss intervals include zero.

Cooperation is much easier on random game splits (combined logistic Brier 0.075) than on complete-family holdouts (0.310). On held-out Prisoner’s Dilemma its Brier is 0.858 versus 0.085 for the stationary Nash comparator. This is a serious structural-transfer failure.

Payoff extrapolation also fails: coordination Brier is 0.465 for the combined logistic predictor versus 0.252 for Nash, on four eligible test games. Narrow supported-domain gains should not be described as unrestricted strategic understanding. This global canonical-parameter holdout also shifts family composition: pilot test games are Chicken and Prisoner’s Dilemma, and Chicken is absent from its training subset. It does not isolate within-family parameter extrapolation.

Game-only and identity-conditioned action predictors are nearly tied in the pilot. Successful known-game model/pair holdouts mainly support a shared payoff response; they do not establish the value of an individualized behavioral representation.

Action-label swaps affect canonical action choice most strongly in equal-payoff coordination games. Aggregate mutual-cooperation and coordination differences are small with intervals spanning zero; this is not an equivalence test.

These are exploratory grouped validations over 24 pilot game shapes. Forecasts for newly generated games have not yet been evaluated. See numerical-interpretation.md and pilot-interpretation.md for support, uncertainty, and scope.
